content: Nucleobases, also known as nucleotide bases, are the fundamental components of RNA and DNA that participate in base pairing. These bases include cytosine, guanine, adenine, thymine (specific to DNA), and uracil (specific to RNA). They are commonly abbreviated as C, G, A, T, and U, respectively. In genetics, these are often referred to simply as bases. DNA contains adenine, guanine, cytosine, and thymine, collectively termed DNA bases, while RNA contains adenine, guanine, cytosine, and uracil, referred to as RNA bases. Uracil replaces thymine in RNA, and the two bases are structurally similar, except that uracil lacks the 5' methyl group present in thymine. Adenine and guanine are classified as purines, which are double-ringed molecular structures, and are abbreviated as R. Cytosine, thymine, and uracil belong to the pyrimidine class, which are single-ringed structures, and are abbreviated as Y. When a base is covalently attached to the 1' carbon of a ribose or deoxyribose sugar, it forms a nucleoside. If one or more phosphate groups are attached to the 5' carbon of the sugar, the resulting molecule is called a nucleotide. In addition to the standard bases—adenosine (A), cytidine (C), guanosine (G), thymidine (T), and uridine (U)—DNA and RNA also contain modified bases that are introduced after the nucleic acid chain has been synthesized. In DNA, the only commonly modified base is 5-methylcytidine (m5C). In RNA, however, there are numerous modified bases, including pseudouridine (Ψ), dihydrouridine (D), inosine (I), ribothymidine (rT), and 7-methylguanosine (m7G). Certain bases, such as hypoxanthine and xanthine, are generated as a result of mutagenic processes, specifically through deamination, which involves the replacement of an amine group with a hydroxyl group. Hypoxanthine is derived from adenine, while xanthine is derived from guanine. Similarly, the deamination of cytosine results in the formation of uracil. The structural framework, or skeleton, of adenine and guanine is based on the purine structure, which is why they are referred to as purine bases. Conversely, the structural framework of cytosine, uracil, and thymine is based on the pyrimidine structure, hence the term pyrimidine bases. The primary bases are incorporated into the growing nucleic acid chain during the synthesis of RNA and/or DNA. Modified purine bases are examples of altered forms of adenosine or guanosine, while modified pyrimidine bases are altered forms of cytidine, thymidine, or uridine. A wide variety of nucleobase analogues have been developed. These analogues are often used as fluorescent probes, either directly or indirectly. For example, aminoallyl nucleotides are employed to label complementary RNA (cRNA) or complementary DNA (cDNA) in microarray experiments. Researchers are also exploring alternative or extra base pairs to expand the genetic code. Examples include isoguanine and isocytosine, as well as fluorescent bases like 2-amino-6-(2-thienyl)purine and pyrrole-2-carbaldehyde. In the field of medicine, several nucleoside analogues are utilized as anticancer and antiviral agents. These compounds are incorporated into viral DNA or RNA by viral polymerases, which recognize them as non-canonical bases. Once inside cells, these analogues are activated by conversion into nucleotides, as nucleosides are more easily transported across cell membranes due to their uncharged nature.
